title: Measuring Verifier Impact in an LLM Generate→Verify→Repair Loop for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We measure how inserting a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair loop changes verifier-detected safety violations of LLM-produced device-configuration proposals. In a preregistered paired design (N = 500 deterministic intent→configuration tasks stratified across VLAN-change, ACL-change, and static-route-change clusters) we compared: (1) baseline — a single LLM proposal (requested model: gpt-5-mini) produced once per task (shared candidate), and (2) guarded — the identical shared candidate validated by a deterministic netops validator with up to one automated repair iteration invoked only if the validator flagged a preregistered high/medium-severity violation on that shared candidate. Primary outcome: verifier pass (no preregistered high/medium-severity violations). Results (complete pairs = 500): baseline passed 499/500 (0.998), guarded passed 500/500 (1.000); contingency: n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002. The preregistered exact paired test was implemented as the two-sided exact McNemar convention applied as an exact binomial on discordant pairs; for the observed single discordant pair this yields two-sided p = 1.00. Paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). Interpretation: under the tested model+validator+shared-candidate regime the LLM produced near-ceiling proposals so measurable verifier+repair effect on the pass-rate metric was small, although the single repair-stage call corrected one concrete baseline failure. All preregistration, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call traces, execution logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the evidence bundle (see execution/raw_results.jsonl and execution/model_configuration.json).

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are being integrated into NetOps workflows to translate operator intent into device configuration, plan multi-step changes, and propose remedial sequences. System reports and surveys emphasize that operational safety depends heavily on surrounding engineering—deterministic validators, sandbox replay, canarying, and rollback—rather than on the model alone [Beckett et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. A common mitigation architecture is generate→verify→repair (G→V→R): the model emits a candidate configuration, a deterministic verifier checks formalized properties, and automated or human repairs are applied if violations appear. Despite conceptual adoption, there is limited controlled, artifact-backed measurement that isolates the verifier’s marginal contribution while holding the model’s initial proposal fixed. We preregistered and executed a paired experiment to answer this narrowly operational question: given an identical initial LLM proposal per task (shared_initial_candidate semantics), how much does integrating a deterministic verifier plus a single automated repair iteration reduce verifier-detected safety violations compared to the same LLM alone? Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired experiment (N = 500) isolating verifier+repair effect under shared-candidate semantics; (2) full archival of prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call logs, and analysis artifacts; (3) a quantitative report of exact paired testing and bootstrap CIs, with operational interpretation and reproducibility guidance.
sections.related_work: Network-configuration verification methods (header-space analysis, route-model verifiers) provide deterministic checks for reachability, isolation, and update safety and are widely adopted in NetOps verification literature [Beckett et al., 2017]. Recent NetOps/AIOps systems propose or instantiate LLM-based intent translators and emphasize validators and guardrails to attain operational reliability (INTA, Confucius, other 2025–2026 system reports). Generate–verify–repair patterns have been proposed across structured-generation domains to reduce incorrect outputs and produce machine-checkable artifacts [PoeTone; INTA]. Independent failure-mode analyses of LLM-driven automation document hallucination, overconfidence, and tool-integration errors and motivate verifier-in-the-loop pipelines [Owen, 2026; DeepSeek-AI, 2025]. However, the supplied literature and system reports rarely present reproducible, controlled ablations that quantify a verifier’s effect size under fixed-model shared-proposal semantics. Our study contributes an artifact-backed measurement in that specific regime, complementing prior system descriptions and conceptual proposals.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design: We preregistered a confirmatory paired design (study_id cand_7f4b9a2d_hosted_gvr_v1_2026) that fixed task-generation seeds, inclusion/exclusion rules, estimands, analysis executor, multiplicity plan, retry policy, and stopping rules before observing results. The primary confirmatory hypothesis: an LLM paired with a deterministic verifier plus a single automated repair iteration will produce a lower verifier-detected safety-violation rate than the same LLM producing a single proposal without verifier feedback (paired within-task). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline where success == verifier reports zero preregistered high/medium-severity violations.

Task corpus and strata: We generated a deterministic synthetic corpus of 500 intent→configuration tasks using deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 with preregistered seeds and stratified allocation: VLAN-change (167 tasks), ACL-change (167), static-route-change (166). Each task defines initial_state, expected_final_state, an explicit required_sequence, and constraints (allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}) to ensure consistency with the verifier’s modeled feature set. The task manifest (execution/task_manifest.jsonl) and representative task payloads are archived in the bundle.

Generation semantics and experimental control: To isolate the marginal verifier+repair effect conditional on identical proposals we used generation_semantics = "shared_initial_candidate" with independent_condition_generation = false. For each pair the pipeline produced a single shared LLM proposal (the shared candidate), recorded it (shared-initial response), and used that same candidate as the baseline output. The guarded condition validated that identical shared candidate with the deterministic validator and invoked a single automated repair-stage provider call only if the validator reported a preregistered high/medium-severity violation. This choice was preregistered to answer the operationally specific question: what safety increment does verifier+single-repair provide when the model’s initial proposal is fixed?

Models, adapter, and validator: Requested LLM = gpt-5-mini called through the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter (provider recorded as openai_responses); model configuration is archived (execution/model_configuration.json: max_output_tokens = 2000, single-attempt generation semantics). Deterministic validator: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 (validator specification and violation-code→severity mapping archived). The guarded arm permitted at most one automated repair iteration per preregistration.

Statistical analysis (confirmatory): The preregistered primary test is the exact McNemar two-sided test on paired binary outcomes. The archived analysis executor implements the common exact-McNemar convention that reduces the paired discordant counts (n10, n01) to n = n10 + n01 and performs an exact binomial test on the observed n10 with probability 0.5 under H0 of symmetry. For a two-sided p-value the executor computes p_two-sided = 2 × min{P(X ≤ n10), P(X ≥ n10)} for X ∼ Binomial(n, 0.5), truncated at 1.0. With n = 1 (one discordant), each one-sided tail probability is 0.5 and so p_two-sided = 1.00; the executor records this convention and the implementation trace in analysis/analysis_log.jsonl. We report this archived exact two-sided p and contextualize it relative to power and base-rate assumptions.

Bootstrap CI: We computed paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CIs for the absolute difference using B = 10,000 resamples, bootstrap_seed = 1729. Resampling unit = paired task (preserving pairing): each resample draws 500 pairs with replacement. Bootstrap parameters and code references are archived in analysis/ artifacts.

Missingness, retries, and stopping rule: The preregistered retry policy allowed up to two automated retries for transient provider errors. The stopping rule completed when the preregistered confirmatory pairs (N = 500) finished or when the adapter model-call budget was reached. Execution accounting and all provider-call traces (including repair-stage calls) are archived (execution/*).
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The experiment completed with complete_pair_count = 500 and model_calls_used = 501 (shared_initial_generation = 500; repair-stage calls observed = 1). No confirmatory pairs were excluded and no provider-call failures remained after retries (execution manifest recorded failed_episode_count = 0). Condition summary (analysis/condition_summary.csv): baseline successes = 499, baseline failures = 1 (baseline_success_rate = 0.998); guarded successes = 500, guarded failures = 0 (guarded_success_rate = 1.000). Paired contingency (guarded × baseline; analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002.

Confirmatory test and CI: Applying the archived exact-McNemar two-sided convention results in p_two-sided = 1.00 for the observed discordant counts (n = 1; n10 = 1, n01 = 0), as computed by the executor. The paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute difference is [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). Both the exact test result and the bootstrap CI are present in analysis/results.json and supporting CSV artifacts.

Repair provenance and the discordant episode: Observed repair-stage provider calls = 1; that single repair produced the sole discordant outcome (n10 = 1), i.e., the guarded arm converted one baseline-detected violation into a verified pass. The execution/raw_results.jsonl file is the deterministic source to locate that episode: filter for pair entries where baseline scoring reports a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass == 0) and guarded scoring reports pass == 1. Because exactly one such discordant pair exists the filter deterministically returns the single episode and its repair-stage provider-call trace, validator violation codes, and repair prompt/response. We do not reproduce full provider prompts or raw traces in the paper body; refer to execution/raw_results.jsonl and the archived validator-spec for the precise violation-code→severity mapping and the repair-stage trace.

Secondary/subgroup analyses and power: Planned per-violation-class secondary analyses were uninformative because observed violation counts were nearly zero across classes; there were no meaningful counts for class-level inference. The preregistration assumed a baseline error prevalence near 0.30 for power planning (N ≈ 384 for 80% power to detect a 10 percentage-point absolute reduction). Observed baseline error prevalence (0.002) produced a ceiling effect that reduced sensitivity to detect small absolute improvements on the pass-rate metric; this divergence between assumed and observed base rates explains the small measured absolute effect despite a nonzero corrective instance.

Representative artifacts and determinism: Representative task payloads, shared-initial responses, baseline and guarded responses, validator traces, provider-call traces, and per-task scoring are archived in execution/ and analysis/ artifacts. Deterministic reconciliation artifacts (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json) record consistent pair and episode accounting and provider-call audit (hosted_model_call_event_count = 501; repair-stage = 1).
sections.discussion:
Operational interpretation: Under the tested regime—single requested LLM (gpt-5-mini), deterministic shared-initial_candidate semantics, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 modeling a constrained feature set (admin, mtu, vlan), and a single automated repair iteration—the LLM produced near-ceiling correct proposals so the measured absolute verifier+repair effect on the pass-rate metric was small (0.002). This numerical finding should not be read as general evidence that verifiers are unnecessary. First, the verifier corrected at least one concrete baseline failure (single discordant episode). Second, in workloads with higher baseline error prevalence, broader verifier coverage, heterogeneous vendor CLIs, or different generation semantics (verifier-guided regeneration, larger repair budgets), verifier+repair gains may be substantially larger.

Design-choice implications: The shared_initial_candidate choice isolates verifier+repair effect conditional on identical proposals; it answers the narrow operational question of marginal benefit when the model’s initial proposal is fixed. It intentionally does not measure verifier-guided regeneration or iterative multi-repair strategies, which are alternative operational semantics and may yield different effect sizes. Practitioners should align evaluation semantics with deployment semantics when estimating guardrail benefits.

Threats to validity: Internal validity is strengthened by preregistration, deterministic seeding, and automated exclusion rules; no manual adjudication occurred. Construct validity depends on whether the verifier’s modeled properties capture the operator’s safety-critical constraints—the pass/fail outcome is defined relative to the verifier-spec archived in execution artifacts. External validity is limited: a single requested model family and single validator on a synthetic corpus constrained to three fields do not support multi-model, cross-vendor generality. Conclusion validity: the very low baseline error prevalence induced a ceiling effect that reduced statistical sensitivity; the preregistered power assumptions did not hold because observed base rates diverged from planning assumptions.

Operational recommendations: (1) Measure baseline proposal error prevalence on representative operational data before investing in expensive automated-repair pipelines—when baseline error is already very low, marginal pass-rate gains from verifier+single-repair may be small for the composite pass metric. (2) Ensure verifier property coverage aligns with operator safety priorities; inspect the archived validator-spec and violation-code→severity mapping. (3) Choose generation semantics (shared-initial vs verifier-guided regeneration) consistent with operational priorities: shared-initial minimizes model-call cost for identical proposals, while verifier-guided regeneration may maximize final-pass probability at higher model-call cost. The evidence bundle includes exemplar repair traces and provider-call logs to support operator evaluation of repair cost vs benefit.

Reproducibility note: All preregistration, task generator seeds and code, model-configuration, provider-call traces, raw LLM responses, validator traces, repair prompts/responses, execution logs, analysis CSVs, and deterministic reconciliation manifests are archived in the evidence bundle. Key artifact paths referenced in the archive include execution/raw_results.jsonl, execution/task_manifest.jsonl, execution/model_configuration.json, analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv, and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl. The initial master prompt for the autonomous run is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA-256 given in the Disclosure Statement).
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment (N = 500) isolating the verifier+single-repair effect under shared_initial_candidate semantics. On the supplied synthetic verifier-scoped corpus and with the requested model+validator pairing, the LLM produced near-ceiling proposals (baseline 499/500; guarded 500/500), yielding an absolute improvement of 0.002 (95% CI [0.0, 0.006]; archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 under the archived two-sided binomial convention). The run demonstrates a ceiling-effect regime in which marginal numeric gains on the composite pass-rate metric are small, while also showing that a verifier can correct rare concrete baseline failures (one archived corrected episode). We recommend that operators measure baseline error prevalence and verifier coverage on representative workloads and select generation/repair semantics aligned with deployment tradeoffs. The full evidence bundle supports deterministic re-inspection of all claims and artifacts.

limitations: Synthetic, deterministic task corpus limited to features modeled by the deterministic validator; task payloads constrained to allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}. Results do not necessarily generalize to unconstrained production intents, cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity, or protocol semantics outside the verifier scope.
Single requested model family tested (gpt-5-mini requested) and single validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) — no claim of multi-model generality is made.

Maximum one automated repair iteration was permitted by the preregistration; different repair budgets, iterative regeneration strategies, or verifier-guided regeneration could change measured verifier impact.

Very high baseline pass rate (499/500) created a ceiling effect that limits power to detect small absolute improvements on the pass-rate metric; the archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 reflects the executor's two-sided exact-binomial convention for n = 1 discordant pair and must be interpreted in the context of low baseline error prevalence.

The single discordant episode (the sole task where baseline failed and guarded succeeded) and its validator diagnostics and repair-stage trace are archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl. To inspect it deterministically: filter execution/raw_results.jsonl for pair_id entries where baseline scoring outcome indicates a preregistered high/medium-severity violation (baseline pass == 0) while guarded scoring indicates pass == 1; because only one such discordant pair exists in the confirmatory set, this lookup returns the single episode and its provider-call traces. The validator violation-code→severity mapping is archived in the execution manifest and validator-spec artifacts in the bundle.
